To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. The poor often prioritise food security and health over global environmental risks.

(1) The risk priorities of the global poor are strongly influenced by their socio-economic status; (2) Poorer groups prioritise household-level risks to their health and food security, while global environmental risks are mentioned by only three wealthy respondents; (3) Risk perceptions vary by gender and age; (4) Poorer groups are more likely to prioritize household-level risks to food security and health than are the wealthier; (5) Risk perception varies by community group and land ownership;
Risk perceptions and priorities vary by socio-economic status (SES), age, gender and spatial/temporal distance of risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of risk perception and behaviour in the global burden of illness and the extent to which these can be changed by education and awareness-raising.
the relationship between wealth, risk and the transition to a late-modern globalised risk society.
risk transition, and how it is experienced at the household level
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“The global poor often prioritises immediate hazards of food and health security over temporally more-distant risks like global warming”.
the global poor often prioritised immediate hazards of food security over temporally more remote risks like global warming, yet this is not always the case.
the risk perceptions and responses of the global poor are strongly influenced by socio-economic status and the temporal and spatial distance of the risk from their immediate environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the global poor are more likely to prioritise household-level risks over temporally more-distant global risks.

the poorest and most marginalised people in India have a much more limited capacity to respond to global risks, such as climate change, than to local and household risks such as hunger, food insecurity and health problems.
risk perceptions and responses are not universal, but are influenced by socio-economic status and education.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the poor are more likely to focus on the risks they can see and feel in the present than those which they can’t, and which will affect their children’s and grandchildren’s lives.
the poorest and least educated groups are most at risk from the immediate hazards of food security and health, and that these risks are not being addressed by the global community.
the poor are more likely to prioritize risks which are immediate, proximate, and directly threatening to their health, livelihood, and well-being.
